title: Why Probability Feels Wrong: The Monty Hall Problem
question: Why do even trained mathematicians confidently give the wrong answer to a simple three-door probability puzzle?
summary: Switching doors in the Monty Hall game wins two thirds of the time, yet intuition insists it is fifty-fifty. The gap reveals how minds reason about information, not just chance.
content:
You face three doors: one hides a car, two hide goats. You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the car is, opens door 3 to reveal a goat and offers you a swap to door 2. Should you switch? Yes: switching wins two times out of three. When Marilyn vos Savant published this answer in 1990, thousands of readers, including professors, wrote to tell her she was wrong.

The Calculation

Your first pick is right with probability 1/3, and that does not change when the host opens a door. The remaining 2/3 probability, held by the other two doors together, is now concentrated onto the one door left closed. Enumerate the cases: if you picked the car (1/3), switching loses; if you picked a goat (2/3), the host is forced to reveal the other goat, so switching wins. Two out of three.

Why Intuition Fails

The mind sees two doors and applies "equal and indifferent" reasoning. But the doors are not symmetric: the host's action was constrained by his knowledge. He can never open your door, and never opens the car. His choice carries information, and ignoring that is the error. If the host instead opened a door at random and happened to reveal a goat, the odds would be 50-50. The same observation means different things under different generative processes.

Bayesian View

Bayes' theorem makes this explicit. The probability that the host opens door 3 is 1/2 if the car is behind door 1 (he can choose either goat door), 1 if it is behind door 2 (forced), and 0 if behind door 3. Weight these by the prior of 1/3 each and the posterior for door 2 is 2/3. Probability is not a property of the doors but of what you know and how you came to know it.

Making the Intuition Work

Scale it up: with 100 doors, you pick one, and the host opens 98 goat doors. Few feel tempted to stay. Studies show that people, and even pigeons, do better with repeated trials, and that natural-frequency framings ("out of 300 games...") help humans far more than abstract percentages. This suggests our probabilistic reasoning is tuned to counting cases rather than updating on conditional information.

Why It Matters

The same structure appears in medical test interpretation, courtroom statistics (the prosecutor's fallacy) and base-rate neglect. Learning to ask "what process produced this evidence?" is among the most useful habits in reasoning.

perspectives.title: Mathematics
perspectives.description: A simple conditional probability result: the host's constrained action shifts all remaining probability onto the other door.

perspectives.title: Cognitive Psychology
perspectives.description: Humans default to treating remaining options as equally likely, a heuristic that ignores how information was generated.

perspectives.title: Bayesian Epistemology
perspectives.description: Evidence must be evaluated against the process that produced it; probabilities are states of knowledge, not fixed properties.

perspectives.title: Education
perspectives.description: Natural-frequency formats and simulation help learners build correct intuitions where formal statements fail.

openQuestions: Is the failure of intuition a bug, or an adaptation to environments where hosts are not so rule-bound?
What framings best teach conditional reasoning at scale?
How should we interpret probability when the same event has different generating processes in different people's minds?
